180: 
181: ### Key Statistics
182: 
183: | Metric | Value |
184: |---|---|
185: | Status | [Current state] |
186: | Version | [Version or release channel] |
187: | Main audience | [Who uses this] |
188: | Operating modes | [Mode count or short list] |
189: 
190: ### How This Compares
191: 
192: | Capability | This Project | Related Option |
193: |---|---|---|
194: | [Capability] | [Current behavior] | [Difference] |
195: 
196: 
197: ---
198: 
199: ## 2. QUICK START
200: 
201: ```bash
202: # Install or prepare
203: [command]
204: 
205: # Verify
206: [command]
207: ```
208: 
209: Expected result: [what success looks like].
210: 
211: 
212: ---
213: 
214: ## 3. FEATURES
215: 
216: ### Key Features
217: 
218: | Feature | What It Does |
219: |---|---|
220: | [Feature] | [Current behavior] |
221: 
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. REQUIREMENTS
226: 
227: | Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
228: |---|---|---|
229: | [Runtime or tool] | [Version] | [Why it is needed] |
230: 
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 5. STRUCTURE
235: 
236: ```text
237: [root]/
238: +-- [path]/        # [Purpose]
239: `-- [file]         # [Purpose]
240: ```
241: 
242: | Path | Purpose |
243: |---|---|
244: | `[path]` | [Role] |
245: 
246: <!-- For items needing more than one line, use the itemized pattern
247:      from Section 4 instead of this table. -->
248: 
249: 
250: ---
251: 
252: ## 6. CONFIGURATION
253: 
254: | Option | Default | Purpose |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | `[OPTION]` | `[value]` | [What it controls] |
257: 
258: 
259: ---
260: 
261: ## 7. USAGE EXAMPLES
262: 
263: ```bash
264: [command]
265: ```
266: 
267: Result: [expected output or behavior].
268: 
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 8. TROUBLESHOOTING
273: 
274: | What You See | Cause | Fix |
275: |---|---|---|
276: | [Symptom] | [Cause] | [Action] |
277: 
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## 9. FAQ
282: 
283: **Q: [Question readers ask often]?**
284: 
285: A: [Short answer with a link when useful.]
286: 
287: 
288: ---
289: 
290: ## 10. RELATED RESOURCES
291: 
292: ### Related Skills
293: 
294: | Skill | Relationship | Use When |
295: |---|---|---|
296: | [`[skill-name]`](../skill-name/SKILL.md) | [Sibling or dependency] | [When to use it] |
297: 
298: ### Related Documents
299: 
300: | Document | Purpose |
301: |---|---|
302: | [`[Document]`](./path/to/doc.md) | [Why it matters] |
303: 
304: ````
305: 
306: ---
307: 
308: ## 7. VALIDATION CHECKLIST
309: 
310: - [ ] README type is correct. Code folders use `readme-code-template.md`.
311: - [ ] Included sections match the audience and task.
312: - [ ] No empty sections remain.
313: - [ ] Commands were tested or marked as examples.
314: - [ ] Links use correct relative paths.
315: - [ ] Frontmatter is valid if present.
316: - [ ] No Table of Contents and no `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments.
317: - [ ] HVR passes: no em dashes, semicolons, banned words or setup phrases.
318: 
319: ---
320: 
321: ## 8. RELATED RESOURCES
322: 
323: - [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) - Code-folder README scaffold.
324: - [`SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) - README workflow and reference map.

327: - [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md) - Human Voice Rules.

59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |

66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |

87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```

128:

131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.

117: - Per-mode workflow contracts never land here, and neither does graph metadata. The hub carries the only [`../graph-metadata.json`](../graph-metadata.json).

45:

48: Phase 1   Implementation
49: Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate
50: Phase 2   Debugging       entered when a check fails
51: Phase 3   Verification
52: done      only with recorded verification evidence
53: ```

63: | 3 Verification | [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md) | Fresh command output, exit codes and the delta from baseline |
64:

70:

94: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-ci/assets/workflow-template.yml` or `job-block-template.yml`, plus the trigger, filter and job-shape rules |
95: | 1.5 Code Quality | The rule index in `sk-code-ci/references/ci-workflow-standards.md` |
96: | 2 Debugging | The failing workflow run and the rule it broke |
97: | 3 Verification | The machine gate the rule index names for each rule, plus a reviewer read for every honour-system rule |

14: # Router Reference - Code Surface Detection
15: 
16: `sk-code` detects the code surface before it classifies intent. It reads the working directory and the changed or target files, because one repository can hold the hub's own code beside another stack.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: This reference gives one detection contract that every sk-code reader applies before it classifies intent, so each route loads the resources of the surface the work actually touches.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Before intent classification, when the request's surface is not yet settled
29: - When a specific surface and SKILLED both match and their order decides which resources load
30: - When a hub surface's `surfaceDetection` block or an external skill's `surface_detection` block is declared or checked
31: 
32: ### Core Principle
33: 
34: Detect **where the work is happening** before deciding which standards apply. The narrowest declared surface that matches leads, and the hub's own code comes last.
35: 
36: ### Surfaces
37: 
38: | Surface | Owns | Does Not Own |
39: | --- | --- | --- |
40: | Specific surfaces | The stack each one declares, such as an operator-private `local-*` skill or a surface packet another repository adds to the hub | Work that matches none of their markers |
41: | SKILLED | The hub's own code under `.skilled/`: skills, agents, commands, MCP servers, plugins, scripts, tests and JSON or YAML config. It is the one fallback surface | A stack a specific surface declares |
42: | UNKNOWN | The result when no declared surface matches | Any standard beyond the universal floor, the quality runner's built-in checks and the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names, each with its overrides applied, until the operator names the surface and its commands. The spec-folder authoring checklist needs the SKILLED surface |
43: 
44: `sk-code-ci` and `sk-code-frontend` are surface packets with no detection block. The hub bundles each from request vocabulary alone, so detection never returns either.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## 2. DETECTION ORDER

34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: Severity tiers exist so reviewers and authors agree on what blocks "done". A rule's tier is a stable contract: the bar does not move per PR, per author or per deadline.
37: 
38: ### Key Sources
39: 
40: - Surface checklists: the checklists each surface declares. For this repository's own code that is SKILLED, under `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/assets/checklists/`.
41: - Rule ids, the hard floor and overrides: [`rule-overrides.md`](./rule-overrides.md) and [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json).
42: - Findings-first review baseline: the `sk-code-review` mode and its review output contract.
43: 
44: ### Design Restraint Ladder (pre-write)
45: 
46: Before writing NEW code for an implementation task, stop at the first rung that holds. Each rung down adds code someone must read, test and keep. The ladder runs AFTER surface and intent routing, so its vocabulary matches the detected surface. It is a post-read reflex: rungs 2 to 5 need you to read what already exists.
47: 
48: 1. **Does this need to exist at all? (YAGNI)** If the requirement looks unnecessary, recommend a scope amendment in the same response. NEVER silently cut scope. SCOPE LOCK and the Logic-Sync HALT still apply.
49: 2. **Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)?** Use it the way the surrounding code does.
50: 3. **Standard library / language built-in?**
51: 4. **Native platform or runtime feature?** Use the native API of the detected surface.
52: 5. **An already-installed dependency?** Never add a new dependency for what a few lines do.
53: 6. **Can it be one line?**
54: 7. **Only then: the minimum code that works.**
55: 
56: Restraint never cuts a P0 item in §3 below, such as input validation, error handling, secrets handling and accessibility, or anything the user asked for.
57: 
58: The ladder consumes the detected surface and does NOT change surface precedence. sk-code-skilled is the fallback surface, always last, and any other declared surface outranks it. Nor does the ladder change the Iron Law: Phase 3 verification is still required. For the over-engineering, gold-plating and scope-creep detectors, see the Restraint Signals table in the repository's `AGENTS.md` and the restraint rules in its `.skilled/repo-rules/`, such as `prevent-overengineering.md`, when present.
59: 
60: ---
61: 
62: ## 2. SEVERITY TIERS
63: 
64: The Code Quality Gate puts every quality rule in exactly one tier:
65: 
66: | Tier   | Handling      | Completion Impact                               |
67: | ------ | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
68: | **P0** | HARD BLOCKER  | Cannot claim done until fixed                   |
69: | **P1** | Required      | Must fix OR get user approval to defer          |
70: | **P2** | Optional      | Can defer with a documented reason. Non-blocking |
71: 
72: **Gate rule**: if ANY P0 item fails, completion is BLOCKED until fixed. P1 violations need explicit deferral approval. P2 violations are tracked but do not block.
73: 
74: Review ranks findings on its own scale, so the review-severity column in sections 3 to 5 maps each rule onto the ids in section 2 of [`review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md). An author can then see how a finding reads in review before review runs. Review keeps its ids, their meanings and its judgement on each finding, so the column is a forecast and never overrides a reviewer.
75: 
76: ---
77: 
78: ## 3. P0 CATEGORIES (universal, apply across stacks)
79: 
80: The universal floor is sections 3 to 5 of this file. Every surface gets it, UNKNOWN included. It holds only rules that hold in any codebase: house style, such as doc-comment forms, typing strictness and naming schemes, belongs to the surface that chose it.
81: 
82: ### Rule ids and overrides
83: 
84: Every floor rule carries an id in the `<class>.<name>` grammar of the [rule overrides contract](./rule-overrides.md) section 3, and an Override mark:
85: 
86: - **FIXED** rules are the hard floor in section 4 of that contract and in [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json). No source changes them, and a `## Rule overrides` section that names one is refused.
87: - **overridable** rules are the default. A repository or surface may set one to `none` or replace it in a `## Rule overrides` section of a checklist file its declaration names, as section 6 of the contract allows. Without such a row the rule applies as written here.
88: 
89: When more than one source speaks to the same rule, the contract's precedence in section 5 decides: the hard floor, then the repository checklist, then a specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then the rule as this file ships it. A surface checklist may still add rules of its own.
90: 
91: ### Mechanical Floor (every surface)
92: 
93: Three faults are P0 on every surface, because no other check can be trusted on a file that has one. The quality runner's built-in checks detect a parse failure in JSON, in JavaScript through both its CommonJS and ESM loaders, in Python, in shell, in YAML and in TOML. The YAML check parses through PyYAML and the TOML check through `tomllib`, and each runs only when the `python3` in use imports its parser. When one cannot, that check reads `SKIPPED_ABSENT` with a `repair` naming what to install, and the run stays verified because neither check is required. They also detect the conflict markers and the credential signature over every readable text file. A parse check for any language outside that list stays with the surface checklist or a configured `syntax-*` check, so no surface restates what the runner already covers.
94: 
95: | Id | Override | Rule | Review severity |
96: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
97: | `syntax.*` | FIXED | **Parse failure**: the file does not parse in its language, which a shebang decides before the extension. A finding in plain JavaScript is heuristic and does not block, because a `.js` file may hold JSX or Flow, and a finding in a `.json` file that parses only once its comments and trailing commas are stripped is heuristic too, because the tool that reads it may accept them. The agent confirms either finding first. | P1, once a heuristic finding is confirmed |
98: | `conflict.*` | FIXED | **Merge-conflict markers**: a text file holds the lines of an unresolved merge conflict. | P1 |
99: | `secret.*` | FIXED | **Credential signature**: a file holds a private-key header or a token in a known credential format. | P0 |
100: 
101: ### Categories
102: 
103: P0 covers issues that have caused production incidents or reviewer-author confusion:
104: 
105: | Id | Override | Rule | Review severity |
106: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
107: | `floor.initialization-safety` | FIXED | **Initialization safety**: code that sets up state guards against double initialization, race conditions and partial loads. | P1. P0 when the gap is exploitable or causes data loss |
108: | `floor.input-validation` | FIXED | **Input validation**: every external input (function parameters, API responses, file contents, env vars) is validated at the boundary. | P1. P0 when the gap is exploitable or causes data loss |
109: | `floor.commented-out-code` | overridable | **No commented-out code**: delete it. Commented code rots and misleads readers. | P1 |
110: | `floor.silent-failures` | FIXED | **No silent failures**: an exception either reaches the caller or is logged with enough context to debug it. | P1 |
111: | `floor.hardcoded-secrets` | FIXED | **No hardcoded secrets**: credentials, API keys and tokens never sit inline. They come from env vars or a secret store. | P0 |
112: | `floor.ephemeral-pointers` | overridable | **No ephemeral-artifact pointers in comments**: a comment never names a spec folder, a packet, phase, task, checklist or requirement id, a feature-catalog entry, an ADR id or a ticket id. Those get renamed or archived and leave a dangling pointer. Keep the durable WHY. The full contract is "No ephemeral-artifact pointers" in `code-style-guide.md` §4. | P1 |
113: | `floor.accessibility` | FIXED | **Accessibility** (user-facing UI): interactive elements stay keyboard-operable, carry an accessible name and keep a visible focus state. | P1 |
114: 
115: `floor.ephemeral-pointers` is the judgment half of a rule the runner also checks. Its machine half is the comment-hygiene checker, whose findings carry the `hygiene.*` ids of `runner-contract.md` section 5, such as `hygiene.issue`, `hygiene.task`, `hygiene.adr` and `hygiene.spec-path`. A `replace:` row never reaches the runner's check.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## 4. P1 CATEGORIES (universal)
120: 
121: P1 covers issues that degrade maintainability or reliability:
122: 
123: | Id | Override | Rule | Review severity |
124: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
125: | `floor.boundary-tests` | overridable | **Test coverage at boundaries**: happy path plus at least one edge case per public surface. | P1 |
126: | `floor.error-messages` | overridable | **Error message quality**: every error carries enough context for the operator to act. | P2 |
127: | `floor.resource-cleanup` | FIXED | **Resource cleanup**: file handles, network connections, subscriptions, observers and timers close or cancel deterministically. | P1 |
128: | `floor.type-safety` | overridable | **Type checks pass**: where the repository runs a type checker, the change passes it. How strict the types must be is the surface's rule. | P1 when the type check fails, P2 otherwise |
129: | `floor.naming` | overridable | **Naming convention adherence**: names follow the convention the repository or its surface declares. | P2 |
130: 
131: ---
132: 
133: ## 5. P2 CATEGORIES (universal)
134: 
135: P2 covers issues that improve quality but do not affect correctness or maintainability:
136: 
137: | Id | Override | Rule | Review severity |
138: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
139: | `floor.documentation` | overridable | **Documentation where it earns its place**: a non-obvious contract or a complex algorithm carries a comment that explains WHY. Whether public APIs carry doc comments, and in which form, is the surface's rule. | P2 |
140: | `floor.idiomatic` | overridable | **Idiomatic refinements**: code follows community style guides and project conventions. | P2 |
141: | `floor.performance-polish` | overridable | **Performance polish**: optimization beyond the NFR targets. | P2 |
142: | `floor.extra-tests` | overridable | **Test coverage beyond boundaries**: extra edge cases, fuzz tests and property tests. | P2 |
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 6. SURFACE-SPECIFIC CHECKLISTS
147: 
148: Each surface adds its own rules to these universal tiers and gives each rule a tier. This file is the contract, and the surface checklists are the implementations. A surface checklist may also carry a `## Rule overrides` section for an overridable floor id, under the precedence in section 3.
149: 
150: | Surface | Phase 1.5 source | Notes |
151: | ------- | ---------------- | ----- |
152: | SKILLED | `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/assets/checklists/` | The fallback. The SKILLED house checklist, `universal-checklist.md`, plus one per touched language (JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Shell, Rust, JSON/JSONC), the JavaScript and CSS house style under `js-css-style/` and authoring checklists for agents, commands, skills and MCP servers. It carries the doc-comment, typing and naming detail this floor leaves to the surface |
153: | CI | `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-ci/references/ci-workflow-standards.md` | Rule index for GitHub Actions workflows |
154: | Frontend | None. `sk-code-frontend` ships no checklist | Web and Figma-to-code practice as read-only references. A file it covers gets this universal floor through `sk-code-quality`, plus the SKILLED or declared surface its path resolves to |
155: | Declared specific surface | The standards its skill ships | Declared through `surface_detection` in that skill's `graph-metadata.json`. Outranks SKILLED |
156: | UNKNOWN | The universal floor in sections 3 to 5, the quality runner's built-in checks and the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names, each with its overrides applied | sk-code does not own Go, React/Next.js server code, generic Node.js, React Native or Swift. Apply those, then ask for the surface and its commands. The spec-folder authoring checklist applies only where the SKILLED surface resolves, and no discovered command applies |
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 7. WORKFLOW
161: 
162: At the Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate:
163: 
164: 1. Identify the file type and code surface. The smart router does this, and `../stack-detection.md` holds the detection order.
165: 2. Run the quality runner on the changed files before committing:
166:    ```bash
167:    node .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/scripts/quality-gate.cjs
168:    ```
169:    It reads the working-tree change by default, or `--files <path>...`, and prints one verdict. Its built-in checks cover the mechanical floor in §3, and the comment-hygiene checker is one of its sensors, so one run checks both. Zero blocking findings are required. `BLOCKED` stops completion until the finding is fixed, and `UNVERIFIED` or `NOTHING_CHECKED` never reads as clean. To suppress a known comment-hygiene false positive, put `hygiene-ok` on that comment line. The gate values and the verdict fields are in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`.
170: 
171:    A repository may also enforce comment hygiene outside the runner: at write time, at commit time and in CI. The verdict's `layers` field reports what a probe found for each of those layers, and a quality claim cites that field. This repository's own wiring is listed under "Comment-Hygiene Enforcement Gates" in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/SKILL.md`.
172: 
173: 3. Load the matching surface checklist from §6.
174: 4. Check every P0 item and fix each failure before going on.
175: 5. Check every P1 item. Fix it or record the approved deferral.
176: 6. Check every P2 item and track misses for follow-up. They do not block.
177: 7. Mark each checklist item `[x]` with evidence: the code that passes the rule or the test that proves it.
178: 8. Go to Phase 2 (Debugging) when a check fails, otherwise to Phase 3 (Verification).
179: 
180: ---
181: 
182: ## 8. RELATIONSHIP TO `sk-code`'s CODE-REVIEW MODE
183: 
184: The `sk-code-quality` mode produces **surface compliance evidence** at Phase 1.5, where the author checks their own change. The `sk-code-review` mode owns the **findings-first review output**: severity-ranked findings, risk reporting and the security and correctness minimums.
185: 
186: Use `sk-code-review` when:
187: 
188: - A PR or a stakeholder needs a structured, severity-ranked findings report.
189: - Security or correctness minimums need an audit.
190: 
191: Use `sk-code-quality` when:
192: 
193: - You are the author checking your own implementation before claiming done.
194: - You need surface-specific quality rules during development.
195: 
196: Both modes rank against these tiers, so author evidence and review findings add up to one quality story.
197: 
198: ---
199: 
200: ## 9. RELATED RESOURCES
201: 
202: - [`./rule-overrides.md`](./rule-overrides.md) - the override contract: the rule id grammar, the hard floor, precedence and how an override is recorded.
203: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/code-style-guide.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/code-style-guide.md) - language-agnostic naming, formatting and structure principles.
204: - [`../stack-detection.md`](../stack-detection.md) - surface detection order, with specific surfaces first and the SKILLED fallback last.
205: - [`../workflow-implement.md`](../workflow-implement.md) - Phase 1, where the Design Restraint Ladder is applied.
206: - [`../workflow-debug.md`](../workflow-debug.md) - root-cause analysis and command-failure recovery when Phase 1.5 fails and the fix is not obvious.
207: - [`../workflow-verify.md`](../workflow-verify.md) - the pre-claim gate that runs after Phase 1.5 clears, before any "done" claim.
208: - [`../phase-detection.md`](../phase-detection.md) - Phase 1.5 position in the sk-code lifecycle.

141: | `floor.performance-polish` | overridable | **Performance polish**: optimization beyond the NFR targets. | P2 |
142: | `floor.extra-tests` | overridable | **Test coverage beyond boundaries**: extra edge cases, fuzz tests and property tests. | P2 |
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 6. SURFACE-SPECIFIC CHECKLISTS
147: 
148: Each surface adds its own rules to these universal tiers and gives each rule a tier. This file is the contract, and the surface checklists are the implementations. A surface checklist may also carry a `## Rule overrides` section for an overridable floor id, under the precedence in section 3.
149: 
150: | Surface | Phase 1.5 source | Notes |
151: | ------- | ---------------- | ----- |
152: | SKILLED | `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/assets/checklists/` | The fallback. 153: | CI | `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-ci/references/ci-workflow-standards.md` | Rule index for GitHub Actions workflows |

Apply those, then ask for the surface and its commands. The spec-folder authoring checklist applies only where the SKILLED surface resolves, and no discovered command applies |
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 7. WORKFLOW
161: 
162: At the Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate:
163: 
164: 1. Identify the file type and code surface. The smart router does this, and `../stack-detection.md` holds the detection order.
165: 2. Run the quality runner on the changed files before committing:
166:    ```bash
167:    node .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/scripts/quality-gate.cjs
168:    ```
169:    It reads the working-tree change by default, or `--files <path>...`, and prints one verdict. Its built-in checks cover the mechanical floor in §3, and the comment-hygiene checker is one of its sensors, so one run checks both. Zero blocking findings are required. `BLOCKED` stops completion until the finding is fixed, and `UNVERIFIED` or `NOTHING_CHECKED` never reads as clean. To suppress a known comment-hygiene false positive, put `hygiene-ok` on that comment line. The gate values and the verdict fields are in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`.
170: 
171:    A repository may also enforce comment hygiene outside the runner: at write time, at commit time and in CI. The verdict's `layers` field reports what a probe found for each of those layers, and a quality claim cites that field. This repository's own wiring is listed under "Comment-Hygiene Enforcement Gates" in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/SKILL.md`.

173: 3. Load the matching surface checklist from §6.

182: ## 8. RELATIONSHIP TO `sk-code`'s CODE-REVIEW MODE
183: 
184: The `sk-code-quality` mode produces **surface compliance evidence** at Phase 1.5, where the author checks their own change. The `sk-code-review` mode owns the **findings-first review output**: severity-ranked findings, risk reporting and the security and correctness minimums.
185: 
186: Use `sk-code-review` when:
187: 
188: - A PR or a stakeholder needs a structured, severity-ranked findings report.
189: - Security or correctness minimums need an audit.
190: 
191: Use `sk-code-quality` when:

193: - You are the author checking your own implementation before claiming done.
194: - You need surface-specific quality rules during development.

196: Both modes rank against these tiers, so author evidence and review findings add up to one quality story.
197:

15: # Rule Overrides Contract
16: 
17: How a repository or a surface drops or replaces a sk-code rule, and which rules no one can change.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Each repository keeps its own house style. One wants almost no inline comments, and another wants a comment on every function. The quality mode and the review mode ship default rules, and this contract is how a repository or a surface says "not here" or "this instead" for one of them. Both modes read the same section in the same files, so a rule dropped for quality does not come back as a review finding.
26: 
27: ### Core Principle
28: 
29: A repository may change any rule except the hard floor. The floor holds the rules whose breach causes an incident in any codebase, and the review severity scale that every finding is ranked on.
30: 
31: ### Scope
32: 
33: This file defines the format, the ids, the floor, the precedence and how an applied override is recorded. The quality and review modes adopt it in their own contracts. The review mode applies the rows it reads and records them on its `Rule sources` line. The quality runner reads the section of every checklist it loads through the same linter, applies and records the rows as section 7 describes, and shows the parsed rows and the conflicts in its explain output. Its registry of known rule ids is read from the documents that declare them, and `commentHygiene.disableRules` carries the machine-checked half. A mode that does not state that it reads overrides behaves as before.
34: 
35: ### Key Sources
36: 
37: - [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json): the machine-readable hard floor and the machine-checked classes. The linter reads it, and sections 2 and 4 of this file mirror it.
38: - [`../../scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs`](../../scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs): the linter that checks a section.
39: - [`../../scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs`](../../scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs): the registry of rule ids the quality runner checks a row's id against.
40: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md) section 5: the `<class>.<name>` rule id grammar this contract reuses.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. THE SECTION AND ITS ROWS
45: 
46: An override lives in an optional section of a checklist file. The heading reads `## Rule overrides`. A checklist that numbers its headings in upper case may write `## 7. RULE OVERRIDES`, and the linter reads both. The section runs to the next H1 or H2 heading. A file carries at most one.
47: 
48: The section holds one table with three columns:
49: 
50: ```markdown
51: ## Rule overrides
52: 
53: | Rule | Action | Reason |
54: | --- | --- | --- |
55: | `floor.documentation` | none | Public functions carry no doc comments here |
56: | `review.function-length` | replace: A function stays under 60 lines | The team's own limit |
57: ```
58: 
59: | Column | Required | Meaning |
60: | --- | --- | --- |
61: | Rule | Yes | One rule id from section 3. Backticks are optional |
62: | Action | Yes | `none` drops the rule. `replace: <text>` puts the text in its place, with the same severity |
63: | Reason | No | Why the repository differs. A reviewer reads it when the override is recorded |
64: 
65: A row names a single rule, and a section names each rule once. Write a literal pipe in the replacement text as `\|`. Prose lines and fenced examples inside the section are ignored.
66: 
67: A row for a machine-checked id (`hygiene.*`, `debug.*`, `dist.*`) changes what the agent and review apply. The runner's own check changes only through `commentHygiene.disableRules` in the repository's quality config. A `replace:` row on a machine-checked id is refused, because no row can rewrite what the runner matches.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## 3. RULE IDS
72: 
73: A rule id is `<class>.<name>`, the grammar of `runner-contract.md` section 5. The class and the name are lower case, and each takes letters, digits and hyphens.
74: 
75: | Class | Names | Source |
76: | --- | --- | --- |
77: | `hygiene`, `conflict`, `secret`, `syntax`, `debug`, `dist` | The runner's own rule names, such as `hygiene.task` | `runner-contract.md` section 5 |
78: | `floor` | One per rule in the universal standards, such as `floor.input-validation` | `code-quality-standards.md` sections 3 to 5 |
79: | `review` | One per rule in the review default lens, such as `review.function-length` | The sk-code-review mode |
80: 
81: A row names a concrete id. A wildcard such as `hygiene.*` is not a row id. The linter checks the grammar, the action and the floor, not whether the id names a rule that exists. Section 7 says what a mode does with an unknown id.
82: 
83: A review check that enforces a rule of the universal floor carries that rule's `floor.*` id, never a `review.*` id, so an override written for the review lens cannot reach a floor rule.
84: 
85: ---
86: 
87: ## 4. THE HARD FLOOR
88: 
89: These ids are fixed. A section that names one is refused. An id ending in `.*` fixes every rule in that class, so a parse rule added later is fixed from the start.
90: 
91: | Id | Rule |
92: | --- | --- |
93: | `syntax.*` | Parse failure: the file does not parse in its language |
94: | `conflict.*` | Merge-conflict markers left in a text file |
95: | `secret.*` | Credential signature: a private-key header or a token in a known format |
96: | `floor.hardcoded-secrets` | No hardcoded secrets: credentials come from the environment or a secret store |
97: | `floor.input-validation` | Input validation: every external input is validated at the boundary |
98: | `floor.silent-failures` | No silent failures: an error reaches the caller or is logged with context |
99: | `floor.initialization-safety` | Initialization safety: setup guards against double init, races and partial loads |
100: | `floor.resource-cleanup` | Resource cleanup: handles, connections, subscriptions and timers close deterministically |
101: | `floor.accessibility` | Accessibility for UI code: keyboard-operable, an accessible name and a visible focus state |
102: | `review.severity` | The review severity ids P0, P1 and P2 and what each one means |
103: | `review.reach` | The review reach rule: a P0 or P1 finding names an input or caller in reach |
104: | `review.security-minimums` | Review security minimums: auth and authorization gaps, injection exposure, unsafe secrets handling and privilege misuse |
105: | `review.correctness-minimums` | Review correctness minimums: regression risk, contract safety, spec mismatch, destructive side effects and boundary handling |
106: 
107: The four `review.*` ids fix the floor of [`review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md): its severity ids and reach rule in section 2, and the baseline security and correctness minimums in sections 5 and 6, which that file says surface guidance cannot relax.
108: 
109: Every other rule can be overridden. That covers comment hygiene, documentation, typing strictness, naming, commented-out code, the `ceiling:` marker and every P2 rule. The list above and [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json) hold the same ids, and a test fails when they differ.
110: 
111: ---
112: 
113: ## 5. PRECEDENCE
114: 
115: When more than one source speaks to the same rule for a file, the higher level wins:
116: 
117: 1. **The hard floor.** No source changes it.
118: 2. **The repository checklist.** A file named in `checklists[]` of the repository's quality config, `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet.
119: 3. **A specific surface.** A hub surface other than SKILLED, or an outside skill that declares a surface.
120: 4. **The SKILLED fallback.** The `sk-code-skilled` checklists.
121: 5. **The default lens.** The rule as the mode ships it.
122: 
123: Two sources at the same level that disagree on one rule for one file are a conflict, and section 7 says how each mode handles it. Two sources that give the same action and the same text agree, and that is no conflict.
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 6. WHERE A SECTION MAY LIVE
128: 
129: A section has effect only in a checklist file that an existing declaration already names. A mode never searches for override sections elsewhere.
130: 
131: | Seat | Declared in | Level |
132: | --- | --- | --- |
133: | A hub surface checklist | That surface's `quality.checklists` in the hub's `mode-registry.json` | Specific surface, or the SKILLED fallback for `sk-code-skilled` |
134: | An outside skill checklist | The `quality` block beside `surface_detection` in that skill's `graph-metadata.json` | Specific surface |
135: | A repository checklist | `checklists[]` in `repository/quality.json`, the `sk-code-quality` packet's quality config | Repository |
136: 
137: A checklist applies to the files its declaration matches by path or extension, and so does its section. An override in a checklist for `.github/workflows/**` never reaches a Python file.
138: 
139: ---
140: 
141: ## 7. READING AND RECORDING AN OVERRIDE
142: 
143: A mode reads a section only through `lintOverrides` in the linter, the same code the command line runs. An override is a judgment the reader must be able to see, so every outcome is recorded where the mode already records its judgment.
144: 
145: | Outcome | Quality | Review |
146: | --- | --- | --- |
147: | A valid row, the highest source for its rule | Applies it and records `override <rule id> <none\|replace> from <checklist file>` in the envelope's `p0_p1_p2_decisions` | Applies it and lists it under `Overrides` on the `Rule sources` line |
148: | `lintOverrides` returns any error for a file | Applies none of that file's overrides and reports the file as `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3 | Applies none of that file's overrides and lists the file under `Refused` |
149: | A row names an id no rule carries | Refuses the file as `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3 | Ignores the row and lists it under `Ignored` |
150: | Two sources at the same level disagree on one rule | Records `override-conflict <rule id> <file> <file>` in `p0_p1_p2_decisions`, keeps the default for that rule and reports the rule as unverified, with no new exit code | Applies the default and lists the rule under `Conflicts` |
151: 
152: The review report carries one `Rule sources` line. It lists the checklist files the review read, then each outcome group, and writes `none` for an empty group:
153: 
154: ```text
155: Rule sources: <checklist file>, <checklist file>. Overrides: <rule id> none from <checklist file>. Refused: none. Ignored: none. Conflicts: none
156: ```
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 8. CHECKING A SECTION
161: 
162: Run the linter on a checklist file before a declaration names it:
163: 
164: ```bash
165: node .skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs <checklist.md> [<checklist.md>...]
166: ```
167: 
168: | Exit | Meaning |
169: | --- | --- |
170: | 0 | Every file has a valid section or none |
171: | 1 | A row is refused: a floor id, a `replace:` row on a machine-checked id, an unknown action, a malformed row or id, a repeated id or a second section. Each problem prints as `<file>:<line>: <message>` |
172: | 2 | A usage error, an unreadable file or an unreadable contract file |
173: 
174: The linter exports `lintOverrides`, `loadContract` and `RULE_ID`, the id grammar, so a reader that checks an id outside a section uses the same pattern. `lintOverrides(text)` returns the accepted rows and every error, and a mode applies the rows only when the error list is empty.
175: 
176: ---
177: 
178: ## 9. RELATED RESOURCES
179: 
180: - [`code-quality-standards.md`](./code-quality-standards.md): the universal floor and its P0, P1 and P2 tiers.
181: - [`../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md): the review severity ids, the reach rule and the baseline minimums that this contract fixes.
182: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md): the runner's rule ids and its envelope.

132: | --- | --- | --- |
133: | A hub surface checklist | That surface's `quality.checklists` in the hub's `mode-registry.json` | Specific surface, or the SKILLED fallback for `sk-code-skilled` |
134: | An outside skill checklist | The `quality` block beside `surface_detection` in that skill's `graph-metadata.json` | Specific surface |
135: | A repository checklist | `checklists[]` in `repository/quality.json`, the `sk-code-quality` packet's quality config | Repository |
136: 
137: A checklist applies to the files its declaration matches by path or extension, and so does its section. An override in a checklist for `.github/workflows/**` never reaches a Python file.
138: 
139: ---
140: 
141: ## 7. READING AND RECORDING AN OVERRIDE
142: 
143: A mode reads a section only through `lintOverrides` in the linter, the same code the command line runs. An override is a judgment the reader must be able to see, so every outcome is recorded where the mode already records its judgment.
144: 
145: | Outcome | Quality | Review |
146: | --- | --- | --- |
147: | A valid row, the highest source for its rule | Applies it and records `override <rule id> <none\|replace> from <checklist file>` in the envelope's `p0_p1_p2_decisions` | Applies it and lists it under `Overrides` on the `Rule sources` line |
148: | `lintOverrides` returns any error for a file | Applies none of that file's overrides and reports the file as `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3 | Applies none of that file's overrides and lists the file under `Refused` |
149: | A row names an id no rule carries | Refuses the file as `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3 | Ignores the row and lists it under `Ignored` |
150: | Two sources at the same level disagree on one rule | Records `override-conflict <rule id> <file> <file>` in `p0_p1_p2_decisions`, keeps the default for that rule and reports the rule as unverified, with no new exit code | Applies the default and lists the rule under `Conflicts` |
151: 
152: The review report carries one `Rule sources` line. It lists the checklist files the review read, then each outcome group, and writes `none` for an empty group:
153: 
154: ```text
155: Rule sources: <checklist file>, <checklist file>. Overrides: <rule id> none from <checklist file>. Refused: none. Ignored: none. Conflicts: none
156: ```
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 8. CHECKING A SECTION
161: 
162: Run the linter on a checklist file before a declaration names it:
163: 
164: ```bash
165: node .skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs <checklist.md> [<checklist.md>...]
166: ```
167: 
168: | Exit | Meaning |
169: | --- | --- |
170: | 0 | Every file has a valid section or none |
171: | 1 | A row is refused: a floor id, a `replace:` row on a machine-checked id, an unknown action, a malformed row or id, a repeated id or a second section. Each problem prints as `<file>:<line>: <message>` |
172: | 2 | A usage error, an unreadable file or an unreadable contract file |
173: 
174: The linter exports `lintOverrides`, `loadContract` and `RULE_ID`, the id grammar, so a reader that checks an id outside a section uses the same pattern. `lintOverrides(text)` returns the accepted rows and every error, and a mode applies the rows only when the error list is empty.
175: 
176: ---
177: 
178: ## 9. RELATED RESOURCES
179: 
180: - [`code-quality-standards.md`](./code-quality-standards.md): the universal floor and its P0, P1 and P2 tiers.
181: - [`../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md): the review severity ids, the reach rule and the baseline minimums that this contract fixes.
182: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md): the runner's rule ids and its envelope.

# sk-doc/shared - cross-packet backbone

## 1. OVERVIEW

`shared/` holds the parts of `sk-doc` that more than one workflow packet needs: the document validators and naming guards (`scripts/`), the standards every packet writes against (`references/`), and the templates and machine-readable rule files those validators read (`assets/`).

A resource earns a place here by having consumers in two or more packets. A resource with exactly one consumer belongs inside that packet.

Nothing here is separately discoverable: `shared/` carries no `graph-metadata.json` and no `description.json`, because it is not a skill and the advisor never routes to it. Requests reach these files through the owning packet, or through the hub `ROUTER.md` `RESOURCE_MAP`, which addresses five of them by a `shared/...` disk path declared in `leaf-aliases.json`.

---

## 2. STRUCTURE

| Directory | Contents |
|-----------|----------|
| [`references/`](references/) | Standards: core structural rules, validation and DQI scoring, the kebab-case filesystem canon, the frontmatter versioning standard, the evergreen packet-id rule, and the hub quick reference. The Human Voice Rules are not here: they have one consumer packet and live at [`../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md`](../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md). |
| [`assets/`](assets/) | Templates and rule data: changelog and frontmatter and llms.txt templates, plus `template-rules.json` and `skill-contract.json`, which are read by code rather than by a reader. |
| [`scripts/`](scripts/README.md) | Validators, naming guards, the frontmatter versioning engine and the semantic rename toolchain. |

---

## 3. HOW PACKETS REACH IT

Packets reference these files by relative path (`../shared/references/core-standards.md`), not by symlink.

The one exception is `scripts/`. Six entries under `sk-doc/scripts/` are facade symlinks into `shared/scripts/`, so a caller can run `scripts/validate_document.py` from the hub root. There is no matching facade for `references/` or `assets/`: the hub has no root-level `references/` or `assets/` directory, so a bare `assets/...` path does not resolve and every reference to these files must be packet-qualified or `shared/`-qualified.

`.skilled/hooks/post-edit-quality/lib/post-edit-router.cjs` hard-codes `shared/scripts/check-frontmatter-versions.sh`, and `sk-doc/scripts/` symlinks resolve into `shared/scripts/`. Moving anything under `scripts/` breaks both.

---

## 4. RELATED

- [`../ROUTER.md`](../ROUTER.md) - maps an authoring intent to the leaf resources a mode loads, including the `shared/...` aliases.
- [`../leaf-aliases.json`](../leaf-aliases.json) - the six alias entries the router addresses as packet-local leaves, five of them `shared/` paths.
- [`scripts/README.md`](scripts/README.md) - per-script purpose and the commands to run them.

# Skill README Template

Use this template for `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`. It writes a skill README in the same narrative voice the repo root `README.md` and the changelogs use: a one-line human pitch, an at-a-glance table near the top, a value-first overview, then quick start, navigation and a verification close.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Give a person a fast, honest orientation to a skill before they open `SKILL.md`. The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.

### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)

The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.

The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.

### Usage

Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.

### Template Focus

The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:

- A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
- An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
- A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
- A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
- Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.

---

## 2. SECTION MODEL

A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:

| # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
|---|---------|---------|-----------|
| 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
| 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
| 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
| 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
| 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
| 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
| 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
| 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
| 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |

`OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.

Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
Add up to two optional subsections after it.
Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
Add the capability section below when it earns a table.

### Capability Section Pattern

When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
State the file or data the skill can operate on.
Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.

```markdown
### The Plugin Knowledge Layer

| Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
|---|---|
| **Beancount Ledger** | append and patch balanced transactions in the structured `.beancount` ledger |
| **Obsidian Tables** | edit `columns`, `rows` and `views` inside `.table.md` JSON payloads |
```

---

## 3. WRITING RULES

- Apply the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist) to README prose.
- State the outcome before the tooling. The pitch and the identity guidance name what the reader gets. The tool names follow as the means.
- Open OVERVIEW with what the skill is and what the reader gets.
- Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to explain a current reader problem.
- Add a short context hook after the blockquote only when it helps the reader. Keep AT A GLANCE as the first numbered section.
- Carry the explanation in prose. Reach for a table only when 4 or more parallel items need a lookup grid (skill relationships, CLI flags, a comparison).
- Use semantic emoji only (✅ ❌ ⚠️ 🔒 🚨) for rules and status markers. Decorative section emoji never: that register belongs to the repository front-page README, while a skill README keeps the technical formatting.
- A short, concrete analogy can carry an abstract mechanism better than adjectives (the repo root README uses "like a lab notebook for software"). Use one only where it clarifies, never as decoration.
- Put the AT A GLANCE table first. Four rows, one line each, no prose cells.
- Name the canonical command or entry point in OVERVIEW or QUICK START so a reader knows where to start.
- Link to real files under `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/`. Verify each path resolves.
- State the expected output for every command you show, so a reader can tell success from failure.
- Be honest about boundaries and trade-offs. If the skill does not own something, say which skill does.
- Keep `SKILL.md` as the runtime surface. The README explains why and how to navigate. It does not restate long reference files.
- Follow the Human Voice Rules. Section 4 lists the banned forms and the scripted checks. It links the full ruleset.
- Vary subsection counts rather than defaulting to three.
- Document current behavior. Keep spec history out of the README.
- Use stable paths and commands. Update the README, its version and its changelog entry when behavior changes.

---

## 4. HVR ENFORCEMENT

Every README this template produces must pass the Human Voice Rules. The full ruleset lives at [`hvr-rules.md`](../../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).

### Banned Forms

The banned forms are: em dashes (U+2014), semicolons (U+003B), Oxford commas (a comma before the final and or or in a list), the hard-blocker words listed below and forced three-item groups.

### Scripted Checks

Run the checks below from the skill root, with the README path as the argument. Each command must return zero matches. The punctuation checks use hex escapes on purpose: the commands stay clean of the characters they enforce.

```bash
rg -n '\x{2014}' README.md
rg -n '\x{3B}' README.md
rg -n ',\s+(and|or)\b' README.md
rg -n '\b(delve|embark|realm|tapestry|illuminate|unveil|elucidate|abyss|revolutionise|game-changer|groundbreaking|cutting-edge|ever-evolving|shed light|dive deep|leverage|foster|nurture|resonate|empower|disrupt|curate|harness|elevate|robust|seamless|holistic|synergy|unpack|landscape|ecosystem|journey|paradigm|enlightening|esteemed|remarkable|skyrocket|skyrocketing|utilize|utilizing)\b' README.md
# Context-dependent words: landscape, ecosystem, journey, unlock, navigating
# Banned as metaphor, allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
```

The word check lists the hard blockers. A hit inside a code sample or a quoted command is exempt. A hit in prose is a violation. Context-dependent words from the full ruleset are banned as metaphor and allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.

# Router Reference - Code Surface Detection

`sk-code` detects the code surface before intent classification. Surface detection uses CWD plus changed or target files because the same repository can contain Webflow frontend code and OpenCode system code.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Core Principle

Detect **where the work is happening** before deciding which standards apply.

| Surface | Owns | Does Not Own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WEBFLOW | Webflow / vanilla HTML, CSS, JavaScript, animation libraries, CDN/minification, browser behavior | `.opencode/` system code |
| OPENCODE | `.opencode/` skills, agents, commands, MCP/server code, scripts, tests, JSON/JSONC config | Webflow/browser behavior |
| UNKNOWN | Fallback for unsupported or ambiguous surfaces | No standards applied until clarified |

`motion_dev/` is a peer resource category rather than a surface. Surface detection still chooses WEBFLOW, OPENCODE, or UNKNOWN first; Motion.dev API, performance, and decision guidance is loaded afterward when the intent requires cross-stack animation context.

---

## 2. DETECTION ORDER

**Precedence**: OPENCODE target/CWD wins over WEBFLOW markers. WEBFLOW wins over UNKNOWN. Use early-return logic — later branches must not overwrite earlier matches.

```bash
# 1. OPENCODE (highest precedence — disambiguates mixed-marker workspaces)
# CWD under .opencode/ OR any changed/target file under .opencode/

# 2. WEBFLOW
[ -d "src/2_javascript" ]
ls *.webflow.js 2>/dev/null | head -1
grep -lq "Webflow\.push\|--vw-" src/**/*.{js,css,html} 2>/dev/null
grep -lqE "window\.Motion|window\.gsap|gsap\.(to|from|set|timeline|registerPlugin)|new Lenis|new Hls|new Swiper|FilePond" \
  src/**/*.{js,mjs,ts,html} *.{js,mjs,ts,html} 2>/dev/null
[ -f "wrangler.toml" ]

# 3. UNKNOWN
# Ask which surface and verification commands apply.
```

**Why OPENCODE wins precedence**: `.opencode/` system tools (e.g. preview servers, mock fixtures, animation demos under `.opencode/skills/sk-doc/scripts/`) may import vanilla animation libraries internally without being WEBFLOW-shipping artifacts. A first-match-WEBFLOW order would mis-route this work to the wrong standards. The target/CWD path is the strongest unambiguous signal of which surface owns the work.

**Generic-Node guard**: WEBFLOW markers are gated to actual Webflow signals (vendor globals, Webflow paths, `wrangler.toml`, `src/2_javascript/`). Bare Motion package imports and generic Motion documentation mentions are MOTION_DEV intent signals after surface selection, not WEBFLOW surface markers. Generic Node.js outside `.opencode/` and without WEBFLOW markers stays UNKNOWN until the user clarifies the surface.

### Explicit Non-Webflow Guards

Prompt-level negative Webflow language wins before WEBFLOW fallback logic. If the user explicitly says any of the following, the surface MUST be UNKNOWN for implementation requests, or N/A for documentation-style cross-stack guidance:

- `NOT Webflow`
- `no Webflow Designer`
- `without Webflow`
- `non-Webflow`
- `vanilla HTML/CSS/JS only`
- `stack-agnostic`
- equivalent wording that excludes Webflow as the implementation surface

This guard applies even when the prompt mentions Motion.dev, GSAP, Lenis, Swiper, or vanilla animation work. Those terms can trigger the MOTION_DEV resource intent, but they must not promote an explicitly non-Webflow request to WEBFLOW.

Expected CS-002 behavior:

| Prompt | Expected Surface | Expected Resource Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `I'm building a vanilla HTML/CSS/JS landing page (NOT Webflow no Webflow Designer involved) and want to add motion.dev animations.` | UNKNOWN or N/A | `references/motion_dev/*` exact files only; no `references/webflow/*` |
| `Show stack-agnostic Motion.dev guidance for animate-on-scroll.` | N/A | `references/motion_dev/quick-start.md`, `references/motion_dev/scroll-and-gestures.md`, exact snippet assets |
| `Update Webflow page code that uses window.Motion.` | WEBFLOW | Webflow implementation refs plus Motion.dev peer refs |

---

## 3. OPENCODE LANGUAGE SUB-DETECTION

After OPENCODE surface detection, select language resources by extension first:

| Language | Extensions | Resource Folder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JAVASCRIPT | `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs` | `code-opencode/references/javascript/` |
| TYPESCRIPT | `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.d.ts` | `code-opencode/references/typescript/` |
| PYTHON | `.py` | `code-opencode/references/python/` |
| SHELL | `.sh`, `.bash` | `code-opencode/references/shell/` |
| RUST | `.rs`; fallback markers `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`; napi-rs/wasm-bindgen vocabulary | `code-opencode/references/rust/` |
| CONFIG | `.json`, `.jsonc` | `code-opencode/references/config/` |
| CONFIG | `.yaml`, `.yml` | `code-opencode/references/config/` |

When multiple languages are touched, load shared OpenCode guidance plus each touched language quick reference/checklist. Rust is a touched-language-set case, not a first-match override: a napi-rs/WASM parity task that touches both `.rs` and `.ts` loads the Rust trio AND the TypeScript trio plus shared guidance, because the Rust module must be verified byte-for-byte against its TypeScript oracle. Cargo markers (`Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock`) are evaluated only after OPENCODE surface detection, never as a cross-project surface signal.

YAML is a live OpenCode config-adjacent genre for command routers, command auto/confirm assets, and workflow contracts. A live-surface scan found 65 YAML/YML files under `.opencode/commands` and `.opencode/skills`, excluding `node_modules` and `dist`.

---

| Context | Expected Surface | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/2_javascript/`, `package.json` | WEBFLOW | Webflow marker wins (no `.opencode/` target present) |
| HTML/CSS/JS with GSAP or Lenis | WEBFLOW | Vanilla animation web signal |
| CWD `.opencode/skills/sk-code` | OPENCODE | Skill/system code context |
| Changed `.opencode/agents/code.md` | OPENCODE | Target file under `.opencode/` |
| WEBFLOW marker (Lenis, GSAP) AND changed `.opencode/skills/sk-doc/scripts/preview-server.js` | **OPENCODE** | Mixed-marker repo: OPENCODE target/CWD takes precedence over WEBFLOW library marker |
| Prompt says `NOT Webflow no Webflow Designer` and asks for Motion.dev guidance | **UNKNOWN/N/A** | Explicit non-Webflow guard blocks WEBFLOW promotion |
| Root `package.json` with no `.opencode/` target | UNKNOWN | Generic Node.js is not owned |
| `go.mod` or `next.config.js` only | UNKNOWN | Go/NextJS placeholder routes were removed |

MOTION_DEV loads from `code-webflow/references/animation/` and `code-webflow/assets/animation/` as a peer resource category. It is not a separate code surface; it supplements WEBFLOW, OPENCODE, or future surfaces when the request needs Motion API, integration, or decision guidance.

Webflow implementation and verification resources remain owned by their corresponding WEBFLOW intents; MOTION_DEV owns only the animation peer resources below.

| ANIMATION / MOTION_DEV | `code-webflow/references/animation/quick-start.md`, `code-webflow/references/animation/animation-principles.md`, `code-webflow/references/animation/animate-and-timelines.md`, `code-webflow/references/animation/scroll-and-gestures.md`, `code-webflow/assets/animation/snippets/principled-reveal.js` |

## 3. SURFACE STANDARDS (the non-negotiables)

- **CDN runtime reality.** Client scripts ship over a CDN with cache lag; treat every deploy as versioned and verify the minified runtime, not just the source. See `references/deployment/minification-guide/overview-terser-and-patterns.md` and `references/verification/verification-workflows/gate-and-automated-options.md`.
- **Interaction-gated loading.** Heavy vendors (HLS.js, FilePond, Swiper) load on interaction/visibility, never eagerly. See `references/performance/interaction-gated-loading.md` and `references/implementation/observer-patterns/mutation-and-intersection.md`.
- **Core Web Vitals are a gate, not a report.** LCP/CLS/INP regressions block; remediate against `references/performance/cwv-remediation.md` and `references/performance/webflow-constraints.md`.
- **Focus and forms are accessibility-load-bearing.** Focus traps and upload flows follow `references/implementation/focus-management/selector-and-focus-trap.md` and `references/implementation/form-upload-workflows/overview-architecture-and-filepond.md`.

# Router Reference - Code Surface Detection

`sk-code` detects the code surface before intent classification. Surface detection uses CWD plus changed or target files because the same repository can contain Webflow frontend code and OpenCode system code.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Core Principle

Detect **where the work is happening** before deciding which standards apply.

| Surface | Owns | Does Not Own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WEBFLOW | Webflow / vanilla HTML, CSS, JavaScript, animation libraries, CDN/minification, browser behavior | `.opencode/` system code |
| OPENCODE | `.opencode/` skills, agents, commands, MCP/server code, scripts, tests, JSON/JSONC config | Webflow/browser behavior |
| UNKNOWN | Fallback for unsupported or ambiguous surfaces | No standards applied until clarified |

`motion_dev/` is a peer resource category rather than a surface. Surface detection still chooses WEBFLOW, OPENCODE, or UNKNOWN first; Motion.dev API, performance, and decision guidance is loaded afterward when the intent requires cross-stack animation context.

---

## 2. DETECTION ORDER

**Precedence**: OPENCODE target/CWD wins over WEBFLOW markers. WEBFLOW wins over UNKNOWN. Use early-return logic — later branches must not overwrite earlier matches.

```bash
# 1. OPENCODE (highest precedence — disambiguates mixed-marker workspaces)
# CWD under .opencode/ OR any changed/target file under .opencode/

# 2. WEBFLOW
[ -d "src/2_javascript" ]
ls *.webflow.js 2>/dev/null | head -1
grep -lq "Webflow\.push\|--vw-" src/**/*.{js,css,html} 2>/dev/null
grep -lqE "window\.Motion|window\.gsap|gsap\.(to|from|set|timeline|registerPlugin)|new Lenis|new Hls|new Swiper|FilePond" \
  src/**/*.{js,mjs,ts,html} *.{js,mjs,ts,html} 2>/dev/null
[ -f "wrangler.toml" ]

# 3. UNKNOWN
# Ask which surface and verification commands apply.
```

**Why OPENCODE wins precedence**: `.opencode/` system tools (e.g. preview servers, mock fixtures, animation demos under `.opencode/skills/sk-doc/scripts/`) may import vanilla animation libraries internally without being WEBFLOW-shipping artifacts. A first-match-WEBFLOW order would mis-route this work to the wrong standards. The target/CWD path is the strongest unambiguous signal of which surface owns the work.

**Generic-Node guard**: WEBFLOW markers are gated to actual Webflow signals (vendor globals, Webflow paths, `wrangler.toml`, `src/2_javascript/`). Bare Motion package imports and generic Motion documentation mentions are MOTION_DEV intent signals after surface selection, not WEBFLOW surface markers. Generic Node.js outside `.opencode/` and without WEBFLOW markers stays UNKNOWN until the user clarifies the surface.

### Explicit Non-Webflow Guards

Prompt-level negative Webflow language wins before WEBFLOW fallback logic. If the user explicitly says any of the following, the surface MUST be UNKNOWN for implementation requests, or N/A for documentation-style cross-stack guidance:

- `NOT Webflow`
- `no Webflow Designer`
- `without Webflow`
- `non-Webflow`
- `vanilla HTML/CSS/JS only`
- `stack-agnostic`
- equivalent wording that excludes Webflow as the implementation surface

This guard applies even when the prompt mentions Motion.dev, GSAP, Lenis, Swiper, or vanilla animation work. Those terms can trigger the MOTION_DEV resource intent, but they must not promote an explicitly non-Webflow request to WEBFLOW.

Expected CS-002 behavior:

| Prompt | Expected Surface | Expected Resource Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `I'm building a vanilla HTML/CSS/JS landing page (NOT Webflow no Webflow Designer involved) and want to add motion.dev animations.` | UNKNOWN or N/A | `references/motion_dev/*` exact files only; no `references/webflow/*` |
| `Show stack-agnostic Motion.dev guidance for animate-on-scroll.` | N/A | `references/motion_dev/quick-start.md`, `references/motion_dev/scroll-and-gestures.md`, exact snippet assets |
| `Update Webflow page code that uses window.Motion.` | WEBFLOW | Webflow implementation refs plus Motion.dev peer refs |

---

## 3. OPENCODE LANGUAGE SUB-DETECTION

After OPENCODE surface detection, select language resources by extension first:

| Language | Extensions | Resource Folder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JAVASCRIPT | `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs` | `code-opencode/references/javascript/` |
| TYPESCRIPT | `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.d.ts` | `code-opencode/references/typescript/` |
| PYTHON | `.py` | `code-opencode/references/python/` |
| SHELL | `.sh`, `.bash` | `code-opencode/references/shell/` |
| RUST | `.rs`; fallback markers `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`; napi-rs/wasm-bindgen vocabulary | `code-opencode/references/rust/` |
| CONFIG | `.json`, `.jsonc` | `code-opencode/references/config/` |
| CONFIG | `.yaml`, `.yml` | `code-opencode/references/config/` |

When multiple languages are touched, load shared OpenCode guidance plus each touched language quick reference/checklist. Rust is a touched-language-set case, not a first-match override: a napi-rs/WASM parity task that touches both `.rs` and `.ts` loads the Rust trio AND the TypeScript trio plus shared guidance, because the Rust module must be verified byte-for-byte against its TypeScript oracle. Cargo markers (`Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock`) are evaluated only after OPENCODE surface detection, never as a cross-project surface signal.

YAML is a live OpenCode config-adjacent genre for command routers, command auto/confirm assets, and workflow contracts. A live-surface scan found 65 YAML/YML files under `.opencode/commands` and `.opencode/skills`, excluding `node_modules` and `dist`.

| CWD `.opencode/skills/sk-code` | OPENCODE | Skill/system code context |
| Changed `.opencode/agents/code.md` | OPENCODE | Target file under `.opencode/` |

| Root `package.json` with no `.opencode/` target | UNKNOWN | Generic Node.js is not owned |
| `go.mod` or `next.config.js` only | UNKNOWN | Go/NextJS placeholder routes were removed |

## 3. SURFACE STANDARDS (the non-negotiables)

- **CDN runtime reality.** Client scripts ship over a CDN with cache lag; treat every deploy as versioned and verify the minified runtime, not just the source. See `references/deployment/minification-guide/overview-terser-and-patterns.md` and `references/verification/verification-workflows/gate-and-automated-options.md`.
- **Interaction-gated loading.** Heavy vendors (HLS.js, FilePond, Swiper) load on interaction/visibility, never eagerly. See `references/performance/interaction-gated-loading.md` and `references/implementation/observer-patterns/mutation-and-intersection.md`.
- **Core Web Vitals are a gate, not a report.** LCP/CLS/INP regressions block; remediate against `references/performance/cwv-remediation.md` and `references/performance/webflow-constraints.md`.
- **Focus and forms are accessibility-load-bearing.** Focus traps and upload flows follow `references/implementation/focus-management/selector-and-focus-trap.md` and `references/implementation/form-upload-workflows/overview-architecture-and-filepond.md`.

# shared/scripts: README Configuration Table Derivation

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

`shared/scripts/` holds maintenance scripts for the `@spec-kit/shared` package. No module in the package imports them, and the environment scan skips this directory, so nothing here reaches a consumer.

Current state:

- `env-reader-table.mjs` collects every environment read in the package, matching `process.env.NAME`, `env.NAME`, `process.env['NAME']` and `env['NAME']` in `.ts`, `.mjs` and `.cjs` files under `shared/`. It skips `dist/`, `node_modules/`, `scripts/`, `*.test.*` and `*.d.ts`.
- Variable names are grouped by the editorial list in `GROUPS`. A variable that list omits falls into a trailing `Other` group sorted by name, and a grouped variable no file reads is left out entirely.
- The script owns one region of `../README.md`, the table introduced by the header row `| Group | Variable | Read by |`.

---

## 2. CONTENTS

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `env-reader-table.mjs` | Scans the package for environment reads, renders the configuration table, checks the README against it and rewrites the table in place |

---

## 3. ENTRYPOINTS

| Entrypoint | Type | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scanEnvReaders(root)` | Function | Returns a `Map` from variable name to the set of reader files, relative to `shared/` |
| `renderTable(readers)` | Function | Returns the header row plus the grouped Markdown rows |
| `extractReadmeTable(readme)` | Function | Slices the existing table out of README text, or returns `null` when the header is absent |
| `checkReadme(readme, readers)` | Function | Returns `{ ok, expected, actual }` by comparing the README slice with the rendered table |
| `node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/shared/scripts/env-reader-table.mjs` | CLI | Prints the derived table |
| `... env-reader-table.mjs --check` | CLI | Compares the README table with the derived one and exits 1 on drift |
| `... env-reader-table.mjs --write` | CLI | Replaces the README table with the derived one |

The CLI runs only when the module is the process entrypoint. That guard canonicalizes both paths before comparing them, because a relative path or a linked directory would otherwise make the script describe itself as merely imported and exit without printing.

---

## 4. VALIDATION

Run from the repository root.

```bash
node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/shared/scripts/env-reader-table.mjs --check
```

Expected result: `README configuration table matches the code.` and exit 0. On drift the derived table is printed and the exit status is 1.

# Workspace: Root Resolution Helpers

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

`workspace/` holds the two root-resolution walks the rest of spec-kit shares. `repo-root.mjs` finds the repository a process may safely write state under. `package-root.ts` finds the skill package directory that holds `shared/` and `runtime/`. Both are pure path walks over `node:fs` and `node:path` with no state, no caching and no network.

Current state:

- `repo-root.mjs` ships as source so build and CI scripts can `require()` it before any build exists.
- `package-root.ts` is compiled and serves TypeScript callers, so the marker set lives in one place.
- Neither module writes anything, and both return an absolute directory or an explicit failure value.

---

## 2. FILES

| File | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `package-root.ts` | Package root walk by marker directories, exported as `findPackageRoot` and `resolvePackageRoot` |
| `repo-root.mjs` | Repository root and source root resolution by authored sentinel, exported as `findRepoRoot` and `findSourceRoot` |
| `repo-root.d.mts` | Type declarations for the build-free ESM resolver so TypeScript consumers reuse the one algorithm |

---

## 3. BOUNDARIES

| Boundary | Rule |
|---|---|
| Imports | `node:fs` and `node:path` only, no dependency on `runtime/` or another shared module |
| Exports | The sentinel and marker constants plus the four resolution functions listed in section 4 |
| Ownership | Root discovery belongs here. Callers keep their own policy for what they write under the root they receive |

The repository walk prefers the nearest directory that carries the authored sentinel, because a bare `.opencode` directory sentinel would be created by a buggy caller and then satisfy every later walk. When the walk exhausts, `findRepoRoot` narrows in this order:

5. Refresh the Hermes skill copies the same way, then commit with the hooks installed, or refresh and copy the manifest by hand.
